meta.title: TIPS Real Yield Curve
meta.revision_note: FRED's H.15 constant-maturity series are not revised after publication.

sources.name: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED)
sources.licence: Public domain (U.S. government data) via FRED; attribution to FRED and the original source requested

inputs.label: TIPS constant-maturity real yields, five tenors (5yr, 7yr, 10yr, 20yr, 30yr)

methodology: Daily real yields for the five standard TIPS constant-maturity tenors (5yr, 7yr, 10yr, 20yr, 30yr), each its own FRED H.15 series (DFII5, DFII7, DFII10, DFII20, DFII30), joined on date. FRED does not publish a TIPS constant-maturity series shorter than 5 years.

These are market-observed real yields on Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities: the yield an investor actually locks in by buying and holding a TIPS to maturity, directly traded and quoted, with no model and no assumed inflation rate. This differs from an ex-post real rate computed by subtracting realized (already-occurred) CPI inflation from a nominal Treasury yield after the fact — that construction depends on which inflation measure and which period you choose; the TIPS market's own real yield does not.
The snapshot chart plots one date's yields across tenors on a categorical, evenly spaced axis (Bloomberg convention), matching the nominal yield curve chart's presentation.
notes: The five tenors do not all start on the same date, and none is forced to: DFII5 and DFII10 start 2003-01-02; DFII7 also starts 2003-01-02 (checked at fetch time — not late, contrary to the pre-fetch assumption that only DFII5/DFII10 were confirmed); DFII20 starts 2004-07-27; DFII30 starts 2010-02-22, reflecting the Treasury's 2001-2003 suspension of 30-year TIPS issuance and later reintroduction. A date's observation carries only the tenors that had actually reported that day; a tenor with no data yet is simply absent from that date's keys, never a null or a carried-forward value. No interior gap longer than a normal weekend/holiday was found in any of the five series' full history as of 2026-09-17.
Values are percent, not a decimal fraction.

A negative real yield means investors are accepting a guaranteed loss of purchasing power to hold the Treasury to maturity — locking in a return below inflation. This happened across most of the curve in 2020-2021.
